cues.text: Born Karol Józef Wojtyła in 1920 in Wadowice, Poland, the future pope endured repeated family tragedy in youth — his mother died when he was eight, his older brother, a doctor, died of scarlet fever when he was twelve — leaving him raised largely by his devout father, whose own austere, prayerful example he later called 'my first seminary.'
A gifted student and athlete with a deep love of theater and poetry, Karol enrolled at Kraków's Jagiellonian University in 1938.

When Nazi Germany invaded Poland in 1939, Karol worked in a stone quarry and chemical factory to avoid deportation, while secretly participating in underground theater as a form of cultural resistance.
In 1942, discerning a vocation to the priesthood, he began clandestine seminary studies organized in secret by the Archbishop of Kraków, unable to attend an official seminary under German occupation.

Ordained in 1946, Wojtyła earned doctorates in theology and philosophy, taught ethics at Kraków's Catholic University, and rose steadily through the Church hierarchy under an increasingly repressive Communist government, becoming Archbishop of Kraków in 1964 and a cardinal in 1967 — building, throughout, a reputation as an effective, quietly determined defender of religious freedom against state pressure.

Following the sudden deaths of Pope Paul VI and then, after only thirty-three days, Pope John Paul I in 1978, the College of Cardinals elected the fifty-eight-year-old Wojtyła — the first non-Italian pope in over four centuries and the only Polish pope in history — who took the name John Paul II .
'Be Not Afraid' and the Fall of Communism

John Paul II's 1979 pilgrimage to his native Poland, drawing enormous crowds despite Communist government disapproval, is widely credited by historians with galvanizing the Solidarity movement that ultimately helped bring down Communist rule across Eastern Europe by 1989.
He survived an assassination attempt in St.

Peter's Square in 1981, later personally forgiving and visiting his would-be assassin in prison, and went on to become history's most-traveled pope, visiting some 129 countries over a twenty-six-year pontificate — the second-longest in Church history.

John Paul II died at the Vatican on 2 April 2005 after a long, publicly visible struggle with Parkinson's disease, canonizing more saints during his pontificate than all his predecessors combined and leaving behind a substantial body of encyclicals, including influential teaching on human dignity and the 'theology of the body.'
Canonized himself in 2014 by Pope Francis, he remains, for many, simply 'John Paul the Great' — a pope whose personal courage helped reshape the map of twentieth-century Europe.
